titre: The Map That Forced Science to Believe in Continental Drift
accroche: A geologist who was never allowed aboard ships drew the proof continental drift had lacked
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1952, at the Lamont Geological Observatory of Columbia University, Marie Tharp draws by hand profiles of the floor of the North Atlantic, one strip of paper after another. She has never been aboard the ships that collected the data: in the 1950s, the laboratory's rules forbid women from sailing on research vessels. Her colleague Bruce Heezen goes to sea and collects the depth soundings; she works through them on shore, alone at her desk. By superimposing six east-west profiles of the North Atlantic, she spots a V-shaped notch that recurs, identical, on every cross-section: a continuous valley, right at the crest of the underwater mountain range the soundings had just revealed.

## A Valley Nobody Wants to See

A continuous valley at the top of a mountain range is not a mere accident of relief: it is the signature of a rift, a zone where the Earth's crust pulls apart. In 1952, the idea that the continents drift relative to one another is a fringe theory, mocked ever since Alfred Wegener's proposal in 1912. When Tharp shows her interpretation to Heezen, he rejects it outright at first. She will recount it herself decades later: “Bruce initially dismissed my interpretation of the profiles as 'girl talk.'”

What makes Heezen give way is not an argument but a second, independent map: that of the epicenters of underwater earthquakes, positioned by other researchers at the same laboratory. The earthquakes line up exactly with the valley Tharp had drawn. A mountain range that trembles continuously along its crest is no longer a convenient hypothesis: it is a measurement. In 1956, the first physiographic map of the North Atlantic, signed with both names, appears alongside a technical bulletin of the Bell Telephone System. The following year, Heezen presents the results at Princeton.

## What a Map Shifts

The ridge that Tharp and Heezen bring to light does not stop at the Atlantic. Extended from ocean to ocean over twenty years of data collection, it traces a continuous chain more than 64,000 kilometers long, the longest mountain structure on the planet, almost entirely submerged. In 1977, the culmination of this work appears as a map painted by hand by the artist Heinrich Berann, *World Ocean Floor*, the first image of the entire seafloor ever produced, which still serves as a visual reference today.

The episode shifts a received idea about scientific discovery: it is not always a flash of individual genius. Here, it is a painstaking work of sorting through data, carried out by someone who was denied access to the field, who supplied the cartographic proof that a theory formulated forty years earlier had lacked. The rift Tharp was the first to see was not invented by her map; it merely ended up, on paper, impossible to ignore.

carte.punch: She was not allowed on the boats. She found the rift anyway.
carte.idee: Marie Tharp draws on shore the soundings brought back by her colleagues and spots a continuous valley at the top of an underwater mountain range: the signature of a rift. Her colleague Bruce Heezen at first refuses to believe it, until earthquakes line up exactly with her map.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Marie Tharp pioneered mapping the bottom of the ocean 6 decades ago
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Places the discovery in the long history of seafloor mapping, up to current expeditions.

quiz.question: What finally convinced Bruce Heezen that the valley Marie Tharp spotted was real?
choix: A submersible dive that made it possible to photograph it directly
The exact match between the valley and the positions of underwater earthquake epicenters
A theoretical calculation published by another laboratory, independent of Lamont's data
Confirmation by the geologist Alfred Wegener himself, consulted on the results
quiz.explication: Wegener had been dead since 1930 and so could not have been consulted; no dive or theoretical calculation figures in this episode. It was the independent map of underwater earthquake epicenters that lined up exactly with the valley drawn by Tharp, turning a contested interpretation into a measurement that was hard to dismiss.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Marie Tharp never go aboard the research ships herself in the 1950s?
choix: The laboratory's rules forbade women from sailing on research vessels
She suffered from seasickness and preferred to work on shore
Her position as a draftswoman gave her no access to mission funding
The Lamont Observatory's ships were already fully booked for several years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In the 1950s, the rules of the Lamont Geological Observatory forbade women from sailing on research vessels, a rule that had nothing to do with the scientific value of her work.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Marie Tharp first spot the valley at the top of the underwater mountain range?
choix: By diving in a submersible herself to observe the relief
By superimposing six east-west profiles of the North Atlantic and spotting a repeated V-shaped notch
By consulting seismic records published by a rival laboratory
By comparing Bruce Heezen's maps with Alfred Wegener's
quiz_supplementaire.explication: By superimposing six east-west profiles of the North Atlantic drawn from Heezen's soundings, Tharp spots a V-shaped notch that recurs, identical, on every cross-section: a continuous valley at the top of the range.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What appears in 1977, marking the culmination of twenty years of data collection?
choix: The second volume of The Floors of the Oceans, signed Heezen, Tharp and Ewing
The official recognition of Wegener's theory by the Geophysical Union
A map painted by hand by the artist Heinrich Berann, the first complete image of the seafloor
The first crewed submersible able to reach the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1977 appears World Ocean Floor, a map painted by hand by the artist Heinrich Berann, the first image of the entire seafloor ever produced, still used today as a visual reference.
